topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: The project contains three copies of a “choose the larger value” function: one for integers, one for floating-point values, and one for strings. A template can share the algorithm, but a naive pointer instantiation compares addresses instead of text. Reuse requires a semantic contract, not just code that compiles for several spellings of a type.

blocks.text: HarborWorks has several functions that select, clamp, or combine values. Copying the same algorithm for int, long, and double creates several implementations to maintain. blocks.text: Deduction does not inspect the function’s intended business meaning. It follows language rules for the parameter pattern and arguments. Read a deduction failure from the call outward: identify each candidate type, the conflicting positions, and whether a conversion should really be permitted. Broadening every parameter until a call compiles can weaken useful type distinctions.

blocks.text: Template argument deduction uses the function’s parameter pattern and the call’s argument types. It does not generally search for every conversion that would make two different argument types fit one T. A call like larger(3, 4.5) therefore needs a deliberate policy rather than assuming deduction will choose the most convenient common type.

blocks.text: One policy is to require matching types and ask the caller to convert explicitly. Another is to introduce two type parameters and choose a result through std::common_type_t, provided the domain and conversion rules justify that choice. A third is to return a selected reference rather than a value, which creates a different lifetime contract. None of these is universally correct; the public operation should state what it means to compare heterogeneous inputs.

blocks.text: An overload set can contain ordinary functions and templates. Overload resolution chooses among viable candidates using the language’s ranking rules; it does not simply prefer the template because it looks more general. A non-template overload can handle a special domain case, as the C-string overload does, while the template supplies the regular typed-value path.

blocks.text: Overloads should remain understandable from a call site. C++20 constraints often express the intended distinction more directly. Chapter 13 shows how a named concept can make a type requirement visible rather than hiding it in a distant substitution error.

blocks.text: The original clamp template uses an arithmetic type trait to reject unrelated types. That trait includes more types than some applications should accept, including Boolean and floating-point types. The body also requires sensible ordering of the bounds and values. A type-level restriction can reject a string, but it cannot prove that a runtime floating-point input is finite or that the lower bound is not greater than the upper bound.

Generic safety emerges from all three layers rather than from a single trait.

reading.title: 11.2.2 Constraining Acceptable Types
paragraphs: The clamp template uses a type trait and static_assert to limit this lesson’s implementation to arithmetic types. It rejects inverted bounds at runtime. For floating-point inputs, its comparison logic assumes an ordered finite domain; NaN requires an additional policy because ordinary comparisons do not establish the expected interval relationships.

A static assertion inside a template body is not the same as a C++20 constraint participating in candidate selection. It can still yield a useful diagnostic after instantiation, but concepts express eligibility more directly. Chapter 13 develops that distinction and combines type-level requirements with value-level overflow checks.

The original clamp template uses an arithmetic type trait to reject unrelated types. That trait includes more types than some applications should accept, including Boolean and floating-point types. The body also requires sensible ordering of the bounds and values. A type-level restriction can reject a string, but it cannot prove that a runtime floating-point input is finite or that the lower bound is not greater than the upper bound.

Separate structural requirements from value requirements. The compiler can check that a type is an integer or supports a comparison expression. Runtime code checks actual bounds and input values. Tests then examine semantic properties such as the output lying within accepted bounds and an already in-range value remaining unchanged. Generic safety emerges from all three layers rather than from a single trait.

Be precise about rejected cases. The supplied example throws for inverted bounds. It is not advertised as a NaN-normalizing floating-point utility. A production clamp for a specific numeric domain should either reject non-finite values explicitly, define their treatment, or restrict the accepted types and inputs so the ambiguity cannot arise.

The supplemental constrained-sum laboratory takes a narrower approach: integral values other than bool, checked representability, and a documented result type. Narrowness is useful when it captures the real application. “Works for every type that compiles” is a weak contract compared with “accepts these types and preserves these stated properties.”
